key_points: SQL databases suit structured data with relationships and correctness-critical transactions — payments, orders, inventory — because they give joins, constraints and full ACID.
NoSQL databases suit flexible or fast-changing schemas and very large horizontal scale — product catalogues, logs, session stores.
Real systems routinely use both: the order lives in SQL while the catalogue and sessions live in NoSQL.
questions.pitfall: 'NoSQL is the modern replacement for SQL.' It is a trade-off, not an upgrade. A payments ledger still needs ACID, and saying so is usually the exact follow-up the panel had planned.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
key_points: Both enforce uniqueness, and the differences are exactly two.
A table has one primary key and it can never be NULL, because it is the official identity of each row and the target of foreign keys.
A table may have many unique keys and they may contain NULL, because they exist only to stop duplicates in columns like email or phone.
State both differences and give the email example — that is the complete answer.
questions.pitfall: 'They are the same thing.' The two differences are NULLability and how many a table can have. Miss either one and the panel will construct the counter-example for you.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a candidate key and how does it relate to the primary key?
key_points: A candidate key is any minimal combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row — a student table may have roll number, Aadhaar number and email as three separate candidates.
The designer promotes one of them to primary key; the remaining candidates become alternate keys and are usually protected with unique constraints.
Minimal matters: if roll number alone is unique, then roll number plus name is not a candidate.
questions.pitfall: Claiming a table can have only one candidate key. It can have several — only the choice of primary is singular, and the word 'minimal' is what the panel checks next.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a foreign key and what is referential integrity?
key_points: A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key of another — dept_id in the employee table pointing to the department table.
Referential integrity is the guarantee that every such value actually exists in the parent (or is NULL), so no employee can belong to a department that is not there.
The database enforces it on delete and update through rules: restrict blocks the change, cascade propagates it and set-null orphans gracefully.
questions.pitfall: 'A foreign key must be unique.' It may repeat — a customer places many orders — and it may be NULL. Uniqueness belongs to the parent's key, not to the referencing column.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a composite key?
key_points: A single key built from two or more columns that identify a row only together.
The classic case is an enrolment table: neither student_id nor course_id is unique alone, but the pair (student_id, course_id) is — one student cannot enrol in the same course twice.
Composite keys appear naturally wherever a table records a relationship between two entities.
questions.pitfall: Calling it 'two primary keys.' It is one key with multiple columns. The enrolment example settles it — say it before the panel has to ask.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Can a table have two primary keys?
key_points: No. A table has exactly one primary key, though that one key may be composite and span several columns.
If other columns must also stay duplicate-free, they get unique constraints — which is exactly the division of labour between primary and unique keys.
questions.pitfall: Answering 'yes, a composite key is two primary keys.' That inverts the definition, and it is one of the fastest ways to lose the panel's confidence on an easy question.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What does NULL mean and does NULL = NULL?
key_points: NULL means unknown or missing — it is not zero, not an empty string and not a value at all.
Because two unknowns cannot be declared equal, NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown rather than true, and rows fail the test.
Every comparison against NULL must therefore use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, and aggregates quietly skip NULLs, which is why COUNT(column) can be smaller than COUNT(*).
questions.pitfall: 'NULL is zero' or filtering with = NULL. Both are wrong and both are tested. Saying IS NULL out loud, unprompted, is what this question exists to check.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Classify SQL commands: DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL.
key_points: DDL defines structure — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.
DML changes data — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
DQL reads — SELECT. DCL controls access — GRANT, REVOKE.
TCL manages transactions — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
The classification matters practically: DDL statements generally auto-commit, which is why a dropped table cannot be rolled back the way a deleted row can.
questions.pitfall: Putting TRUNCATE under DML. It is DDL — it resets the table by deallocation rather than deleting row by row, which is exactly why it is fast and why most systems cannot roll it back.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP.
key_points: DELETE removes rows one at a time, accepts a WHERE clause, writes each removal to the log so it can be rolled back and fires row-level triggers.
TRUNCATE empties the entire table in one deallocation — no WHERE, minimal logging, dramatically faster on large tables — but the structure survives.
DROP removes the table itself along with its indexes, constraints and permissions.
Pick by intent: some rows, all rows or the table itself.
questions.pitfall: 'TRUNCATE deletes the table.' It empties the table — the structure stays and you can insert into it a second later. Only DROP removes the table, and confusing the two is the trap this question sets.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
key_points: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens; HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation.
That order is the reason aggregates such as COUNT or AVG are legal only in HAVING — when WHERE runs, the groups do not exist yet, so there is nothing to count.
In one query: WHERE throws out rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING throws out groups.
questions.pitfall: Writing an aggregate inside WHERE, as in WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 — the single most common mistake in dictated queries. Narrate the order rows-then-groups while writing and the error becomes impossible.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the logical order of execution of a SQL query?
key_points: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

The written order and the execution order are different, and the practical proof is aliases: a column alias created in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE, because WHERE has already run by the time SELECT names anything.
Quote that example and the panel knows the order is understood rather than memorised.
questions.pitfall: Reciting the written order with SELECT first. Execution starts at FROM, and the alias-in-WHERE example is the expected evidence — bring it yourself.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Write a query for the second-highest salary.
key_points: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp); The inner query finds the top salary, the outer finds the maximum among everything below it — so duplicate top salaries are handled naturally.
Mention the modern alternative with DENSE_RANK() = 2 for the follow-up; ranking functions generalise this to any N.
questions.pitfall: Only 'ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1,1' without DISTINCT. Two people sharing the top salary break it, and 'what if two people earn the maximum?' is the prepared follow-up.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How do you get the Nth-highest salary?
key_points: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1; DISTINCT collapses ties so OFFSET counts salary levels rather than rows.
The portable version wraps DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) in a subquery and filters rank = N — worth writing once from memory because it works on every major database.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting DISTINCT. With duplicate salaries OFFSET walks over repeated rows and lands on the wrong value — the tie case is exactly what this question is testing.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Write a query to find duplicate values in a column.
key_points: SELECT email, COUNT(*) c FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING c > 1; Group by the column, count each group, keep the groups larger than one.
The same skeleton answers a whole family of questions — duplicate phone numbers, students enrolled twice, repeated transactions — so learn the shape, not the query.
questions.pitfall: Trying to filter the count inside WHERE. Groups must exist before they can be counted, so the filter belongs in HAVING — say 'group first, then filter groups' while writing.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) — what differs?
key_points: COUNT(*) counts rows, full stop.
COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL, because aggregates skip NULLs.
On a table of 100 employees where 10 have no manager assigned, COUNT(*) returns 100 while COUNT(manager_id) returns 90 — and that gap is the entire point of the question.
questions.pitfall: 'They are identical.' On any column containing NULLs the numbers differ, and the panel usually has the manager example ready. Give it first.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: UNION vs UNION ALL.
key_points: Both stack two result sets with matching column counts and types.
UNION removes duplicate rows, which forces a sort or hash of the combined result and costs time.
UNION ALL keeps everything and is therefore faster.
The professional habit: use UNION ALL by default and pay for UNION only when duplicates genuinely must go.
questions.pitfall: Saying UNION ALL removes duplicates — it is exactly the opposite. Adding the performance reasoning is what upgrades this from a definition to an answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: IN vs EXISTS — when is each preferable?
key_points: IN compares a value against a returned list and reads naturally for small static sets.

EXISTS asks only whether a matching row is there and can stop at the first hit, which traditionally favoured it for correlated checks against large tables — though modern optimisers often rewrite the two identically.
The trap worth volunteering: NOT IN against a list containing even one NULL returns no rows at all, so NOT EXISTS is the safe negative form.
questions.pitfall: The memorised absolute 'EXISTS is always faster.' Optimisers have made that stale. Mentioning the NOT IN with NULL trap instead shows real query experience and usually ends the thread.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
key_points: A subquery that references a column of the outer query, so logically it re-evaluates once per outer row.
The standard example: employees earning above their own department's average — the inner AVG(salary) is computed per department because it refers to the outer row's dept value.
That per-row dependence is also why correlated subqueries can be slow and why panels ask how to rewrite them as joins.
questions.pitfall: 'A subquery inside a query' — that defines an ordinary nested subquery. Correlated means it depends on the outer row, and the department-average example is the accepted proof of understanding.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a view? Can you update through it?
key_points: A view is a stored query that behaves like a virtual table — it holds no data of its own and re-runs its definition every time it is referenced.
Teams use views for security, exposing only permitted columns, and for simplification, hiding a complex join behind a clean name.
Simple single-table views are updatable; views built on joins, aggregates or DISTINCT generally are not, because the database cannot map the change back to base rows.
A materialised view is the exception that does store its results and must be refreshed.
questions.pitfall: 'A view stores data.' An ordinary view stores only the query. Raising materialised views yourself — the one kind that does store results — turns the trap into a strength.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain the types of joins.
key_points: INNER returns only the rows that match in both tables.
LEFT returns every row of the left table, with matches filled in and NULLs where nothing matched; RIGHT is its mirror.
FULL OUTER keeps everything from both sides.
CROSS pairs every row with every row — the Cartesian product.
SELF joins a table to itself through aliases, the employees-and-managers case.
Knowing when each returns NULLs is what the follow-ups probe.
questions.pitfall: Listing only inner and left. FULL OUTER and CROSS are precisely where the follow-up goes, so cover all six unprompted and finish on SELF with its aliases.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: A has 10 rows, B has 5 matching — how many rows do INNER and LEFT JOIN return?
key_points: INNER returns only the matched rows — five if each key matches once, more if any key matches multiple rows in B, because every pairing produces a row.
LEFT returns all ten rows of A: the five matched ones filled in and the five unmatched ones padded with NULLs on B's columns.
Saying the multiplication effect aloud is what earns the mark, because duplicate keys are the follow-up.
questions.pitfall: A bare number with no reasoning. Joins multiply on duplicate keys, and the panel's next line is almost always 'and if B has two rows for one key?' — pre-empt it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Give a self-join use case and the query.
key_points: Employees and their managers live in one table, so the table joins to itself under two aliases: SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager FROM emp e LEFT JOIN emp m ON e.mgr_id = m.id; The LEFT join matters — an INNER join would silently drop the CEO, who has no manager.
Catching that detail unprompted is what distinguishes the answer.
questions.pitfall: Writing it without aliases — a self-join without aliases does not even parse, because the database cannot tell the two copies apart. The aliases are the answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How do you find rows in table A with no match in table B?
key_points: SELECT a.* FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id WHERE b.a_id IS NULL; The LEFT join keeps every row of A and stamps NULL where B had nothing, so filtering on IS NULL isolates exactly the unmatched rows.
NOT EXISTS is the equally safe alternative and reads more declaratively.
questions.pitfall: Only 'NOT IN'. If B's column contains a single NULL, NOT IN returns zero rows and the query silently lies. Naming that trap is why the LEFT JOIN pattern is the accepted answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: When does a CROSS JOIN appear by accident?
key_points: Whenever a join is written without its ON condition — or in old comma-style syntax without a WHERE — every row pairs with every row and a 10,000 × 10,000 join produces a hundred million rows.
That is the classic 'my query hangs' incident.
Intentionally, CROSS JOIN generates combinations: every size with every colour, every student with every exam slot.
questions.pitfall: 'CROSS JOIN is useless.' It is deliberate and useful for generating combinations — the accident is the missing ON condition, not the join type, and separating those two ideas is the answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is normalisation and why do we do it?
key_points: Normalisation reorganises tables along their functional dependencies so that every fact is stored exactly once.
The purpose is correctness: redundancy is what creates insert, update and delete anomalies, and removing the redundancy removes the anomalies with it.
The cost is honest too — more tables means more joins at read time, which is why the question of denormalisation exists at all.
questions.pitfall: 'Normalisation makes the database faster.' It frequently makes reads slower because of the extra joins. The goal is one fact stored once — correctness, not speed — and saying the cost aloud shows maturity.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with an example.
key_points: Take one messy student-course table and walk it up.
1NF demands atomic cells: a phones column holding three numbers splits into separate rows or a phone table.
2NF removes partial dependency on a composite key: in (order_id, product_id), product_name depends on product_id alone, so it moves to a product table.
3NF removes transitive dependency between non-key columns: employee → dept_id → dept_name means dept_name belongs in a department table.
After 3NF each fact has exactly one home.
questions.pitfall: Reciting the three definitions with no example table. The examiner is checking whether you can actually do the decomposition — walking one table up the forms is the answer; the definitions alone are not.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is BCNF and how does it differ from 3NF?
key_points: BCNF tightens 3NF with one rule: every determinant — the left side of any functional dependency — must be a candidate key.

A table can satisfy 3NF and still break BCNF when a non-key column determines part of a composite key, the classic case being a student-subject-teacher table where each teacher teaches only one subject: teacher determines subject, yet teacher is not a candidate key.
Decomposing on that dependency restores BCNF.
questions.pitfall: 'BCNF and 3NF are the same.' Name the gap precisely: 3NF tolerates a dependency whose right side is a key attribute; BCNF tolerates nothing whose left side is not a candidate key.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What anomalies does an unnormalised table suffer?
key_points: Three, and they all come from redundancy.
Insert anomaly: a new department cannot be recorded until it has an employee, because department data lives only inside employee rows.
Update anomaly: renaming a department means updating every one of its rows — miss one and the data disagrees with itself.
Delete anomaly: removing the last employee of a department deletes the department's existence too.
One example table demonstrates all three.
questions.pitfall: The vague 'data gets inconsistent.' The expected shape is the three named anomalies attached to one concrete table — insert, update and delete, in that order.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: When would you deliberately denormalise?
key_points: In read-heavy reporting and analytics, where join cost dominates everything else.
A warehouse duplicates dimension data into wide tables on purpose, keeping the redundancy consistent through the load process, and buys back read speed by touching one table instead of five.
The word to use is trade-off: controlled redundancy exchanged for fewer joins, acceptable because the load pipeline owns the consistency.
questions.pitfall: 'Denormalisation is bad practice.' It is a deliberate engineering decision used in virtually every reporting system. Present it as a trade-off with a named safeguard, never as a sin.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain ACID with a money-transfer example.
key_points: Walk all four letters through one transfer of 500 from A to B.
Atomicity: the debit and the ₹ credit happen together or not at all — a crash in between rolls the debit back.
Consistency: every rule holds before and after, so total money is unchanged and no balance constraint breaks.
Isolation: a concurrent transaction can never observe the half-done state where A is debited and B is not yet credited.
Durability: once the commit is acknowledged, the transfer survives any crash, because it is already in the log.
questions.pitfall: Skipping a letter, or the vague 'consistency means data is correct.' The accepted format is all four letters walked through the same single transfer — practise it as one continuous story.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What do COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT do?
key_points: COMMIT ends the transaction and makes its changes permanent — durability begins at that moment.
ROLLBACK abandons the transaction and undoes everything since it began.

SAVEPOINT plants a named marker inside a running transaction so that ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT can undo only the work after the marker while keeping what came before — useful in long multi-step procedures where one step failing should not waste the rest.
questions.pitfall: 'Rollback undoes committed work.' It cannot — once committed, durability applies and only a compensating transaction can reverse the effect. Rollback operates strictly on uncommitted changes.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Define dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom read.
key_points: Dirty read: transaction A reads data that transaction B has written but not committed — if B rolls back, A acted on data that never existed.
Non-repeatable read: A reads the same row twice and gets different values because someone committed an update in between.
Phantom read: A runs the same query twice and new rows appear because someone committed inserts matching the condition.
Keywords in order: uncommitted data, same row changed, new rows appeared.
questions.pitfall: Mixing dirty with non-repeatable. The separator is commitment: dirty involves uncommitted data; non-repeatable involves committed changes to a row already read. Hold onto the three keywords and they stay apart.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain the isolation levels and what each prevents.
key_points: Four levels, each blocking one more anomaly.
Read Uncommitted prevents nothing.
Read Committed stops dirty reads by showing only committed data.
Repeatable Read additionally locks the rows already read, stopping non-repeatable reads.
Serializable stops phantoms too by making transactions behave as if they ran one after another — full correctness bought at the price of concurrency.
Most production systems run Read Committed and accept the remaining anomalies knowingly.
questions.pitfall: Claiming Serializable is the practical default. Databases default to Read Committed — or Repeatable Read in MySQL — precisely because Serializable is expensive, and knowing the real default is the point of the question.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Shared vs exclusive locks, and what is two-phase locking?
key_points: A shared lock lets many transactions read the same item together; an exclusive lock admits one writer and shuts out every other reader and writer.
Two-phase locking is the protocol that makes locking correct: a growing phase where the transaction only acquires locks, then a shrinking phase where it only releases them.
That discipline guarantees serialisable schedules — but because transactions hold locks while waiting for more, it can also produce deadlocks.
Guarantee and cost belong in the same breath.
questions.pitfall: '2PL means locking twice.' It means two phases — grow, then shrink. State what it buys, serialisability, and what it risks, deadlock; either half alone is an incomplete answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How do deadlocks happen in a database and how are they handled?
key_points: Transaction A locks row 1 and waits for row 2 while transaction B locks row 2 and waits for row 1 — a cycle, and neither can move.
Databases resolve it automatically: a detector finds the cycle in the wait graph, picks a victim, rolls it back and returns a deadlock error for the application to retry.
Applications prevent it by always locking rows in a consistent order and by keeping transactions short so locks are held for milliseconds rather than minutes.
questions.pitfall: Answering only with the operating-system theory of Coffman conditions. The panel wants the database version — victim selection by the engine plus consistent lock ordering in the application code.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a lost update?
key_points: Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value from what it read and both write back — the second write silently overwrites the first, and one update vanishes without any error.
Two counters incrementing a balance of 100 by 50 each should end at 200 but end at 150.
Prevented by locking the row for the whole read-modify-write, or optimistically by carrying a version number and rejecting a write whose version is stale.
questions.pitfall: 'It is the same as a dirty read.' No uncommitted data is involved — both writes are legitimate and committed; they simply collide. The fix is locking or versioning, and naming both is the full answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency control.
key_points: Pessimistic control locks first and works second — nobody can interfere, which is right when conflicts are frequent, but everybody queues.
Optimistic control works without locks and validates at commit, comparing a version or timestamp and retrying on conflict — near-zero overhead when collisions are rare.
The deciding factor is the conflict rate: hot contended rows call for pessimistic locking; web workloads where two users rarely edit the same record suit optimistic control.
questions.pitfall: Declaring one universally better. The answer is a decision rule, not a winner — conflict rate decides, and giving one example on each side closes the question.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is an index and how does it work?
key_points: An index is a separate ordered structure — a B-tree or B+ tree — that maps key values to row locations, turning a full-table scan of O(n) into a tree descent of O(log n).
In a B+ tree all data pointers sit in the leaf level and the leaves are linked in order, which is why range queries such as BETWEEN run so well.
The price is paid on writes: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must maintain every index on the table, and each index consumes storage.
questions.pitfall: 'An index makes the database faster.' Reads, yes — writes, no. An answer that does not state the write cost and the storage cost is treated as half an answer, because the follow-up is always the cost.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Clustered vs non-clustered index — explain both.
key_points: A clustered index determines the physical order of the table itself — the rows are the leaf level, so there can be exactly one per table and it is usually the primary key.
A non-clustered index is a separate structure whose leaves point back to the rows, so a table may carry many.
Practical consequence: a range scan on the clustered key reads rows that sit next to each other on disk, which is why the choice of clustering key matters.
questions.pitfall: 'A table can have several clustered indexes.' Rows can be physically ordered only one way, so exactly one — and explaining why with the physical-order argument is what the question wants.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: When do indexes hurt performance?
key_points: Four situations worth naming.
Write-heavy tables, because every write maintains every index.
Very small tables, where a full scan is cheaper than a tree descent.
Low-selectivity columns such as gender, where the index narrows almost nothing.
And queries that wrap the indexed column in a function — WHERE YEAR(join_date) = 2025 — which blinds the index entirely; rewrite the predicate as a range instead.
questions.pitfall: 'Add indexes everywhere.' This question screens for exactly the opposite instinct — the cases where an index is pure cost. Naming all four situations, with the function-on-column rewrite, is the complete answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are composite and covering indexes?
key_points: A composite index spans multiple columns and obeys the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (dept, salary) serves queries filtering on dept, or dept and salary together, but not salary alone — the order of columns is the whole design decision.
A covering index contains every column a query touches, so the database answers from the index alone and never visits the table, which is the single cheapest read there is.
questions.pitfall: 'Column order in a composite index does not matter.' The leftmost-prefix rule is the entire game, and it is the phrase the panel is waiting to hear.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Stored procedure vs function vs trigger.
key_points: A stored procedure is a named block of SQL kept in the database and called explicitly — it may modify data, return many results and hold business logic close to the data.
A function returns a single value and is designed to be used inside queries, so it should not modify data.

A trigger is code the database fires automatically on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE — nobody calls it, which is both its power for auditing and its danger, because logic hides where developers do not look.
questions.pitfall: 'A trigger is a procedure you call on events.' Nobody calls a trigger — automatic firing is its defining property, and mentioning the hidden-logic danger earns the extra mark.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: A query is slow — walk me through how you would optimise it.
key_points: Diagnose before treating. First read the execution plan with EXPLAIN and find where the time actually goes — a full scan, a bad join order, a missing index.

Then, in order: create or fix the index the WHERE and JOIN columns need, select only the columns required instead of *, rewrite non-sargable predicates so functions come off the column, verify statistics are fresh so the optimiser chooses well and check whether the query can be restructured.
Only after the query level is exhausted do denormalisation or caching enter the conversation.
questions.pitfall: Jumping straight to 'add an index.' The accepted first move is reading the execution plan — an answer that starts with EXPLAIN signals real debugging experience; an answer that starts with the index signals guesswork.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, DBMS and SQL (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why OOP at all?
key_points: Four clauses. It models real entities as objects with state and behaviour, so code mirrors the problem.
It reuses through inheritance, so common behaviour is written once.
It changes safely through encapsulation, because internals can evolve behind a stable interface.
And it extends through polymorphism, because new types plug in where old ones worked.
Each clause is a pillar earning its keep.
questions.pitfall: 'Because it organises code better.' The four-clause answer — model, reuse, safe change, extension — is the accepted shape, and it doubles as a map of the pillars.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Class vs object.
key_points: A class is the blueprint: it defines the fields and methods but occupies no memory for instance data.
An object is one instance built from that blueprint, with its own state in memory.
One class, many objects — two Account objects share the definition of deposit but hold different balances.
Blueprint against instance is the whole answer.
questions.pitfall: 'A class is a collection of objects.' It is the definition objects are created from — a drawing of a house is not a housing colony.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Name the four pillars in one breath each.
key_points: Encapsulation: data and the methods that guard it bundled together, accessed only through the interface.
Abstraction: expose what it does, hide how.
Inheritance: a child reuses and extends a parent — the is-a relationship.
Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours depending on the actual object.
Each then needs an example from your own project ready for the follow-up.
questions.pitfall: Definitions without examples on standby. 'Give me an example from your project' follows immediately, and an improvised example is where this question is lost.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain encapsulation with a concrete example.
key_points: Bundle the data with the only methods allowed to touch it and make the data private: an Account keeps balance private and exposes deposit and withdraw, which validate every change.
Nobody can set the balance to a negative number from outside because no outside path to it exists.
The class's internals can later change entirely without breaking any caller.
questions.pitfall: 'Encapsulation is making variables private.' Private is the mechanism; the idea is a guarded single point of change — the validation inside deposit is the point.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain abstraction, and how is it different from encapsulation?
key_points: Abstraction is exposing what something does while hiding how — car.start() without piston details; a List interface without caring whether an array or nodes sit behind it.
The difference: abstraction is a design-level idea about hiding complexity behind an interface; encapsulation is the implementation-level bundling and guarding of data.
Abstraction hides complexity; encapsulation hides and protects state.
questions.pitfall: Answering that they are the same thing at different words. Hiding complexity against protecting state is the accepted separation — one design-level, one code-level.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is inheritance and what are its types?
key_points: A child class acquires the fields and methods of a parent and may add or override — the is-a relationship: SavingsAccount extends Account.
Types: single, multilevel (A to B to C), hierarchical (one parent, many children) and multiple — which Java forbids for classes because of the diamond ambiguity, allowing it only through interfaces.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the Java multiple-inheritance position. 'Not for classes, yes through interfaces, because of the diamond problem' is the follow-up — pre-empt it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is polymorphism and what are its two kinds?
key_points: One call, many behaviours: area() invoked on a Shape reference runs Circle's or Square's version depending on the actual object.

Two kinds: compile-time polymorphism through overloading, resolved by the compiler from parameter lists, and runtime polymorphism through overriding, resolved by dynamic dispatch from the object's real type.
The reference type decides what compiles; the object type decides what runs.
questions.pitfall: Merging the kinds. Compile-time equals overloading, runtime equals overriding — and the reference-versus-object line is the sentence that proves it is understood.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is dynamic dispatch?
key_points: The runtime mechanism behind overriding: when a method is called through a base-class reference, the JVM looks at the actual object's type and runs that class's version — Shape s = new Circle(); s.area() runs Circle's area.
It is what makes code written against the parent automatically correct for every future child.
questions.pitfall: 'The compiler picks the method.' For overridden methods the decision happens at runtime from the object — that timing is the entire concept.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Overloading vs overriding — the complete answer.
key_points: Overloading: same method name, different parameter lists, in the same class — resolved at compile time from the arguments; return type alone cannot overload.
Overriding: same signature redefined in a child class — resolved at runtime through dynamic dispatch.
So overloading is convenience naming decided by the compiler; overriding is behavioural replacement decided by the object.
questions.pitfall: 'Overloading is runtime polymorphism' — the single most common OOP error we hear. Overloading binds at compile time; only overriding is runtime.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are the rules for a valid override?
key_points: Same name and parameter list; the return type must be the same or a subtype (covariant); access cannot be narrower than the parent's — a public method cannot become protected; and the override cannot throw broader checked exceptions.
The compiler enforces all of it, and the @Override annotation catches accidental mismatches.
questions.pitfall: Believing anything with the same name overrides. The access-cannot-narrow and exception rules are the tested edges, and @Override is the professional habit to mention.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is an abstract class?
key_points: A class that cannot be instantiated and may mix abstract methods — declared without bodies, which children must implement — with concrete methods and state.
It is the tool for a family of related classes sharing code and fields: Account holds the balance logic while leaving interestRate() abstract for each account type to define.
questions.pitfall: 'A class with only abstract methods.' It may hold concrete methods, fields and even constructors — partial implementation is precisely its value.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is an interface?
key_points: A pure contract: a set of method signatures a class promises to implement, with no instance state.
A class can implement many interfaces, which is how Java delivers multiple inheritance of type — Comparable, Serializable and your own capability in one class.
Since Java 8 interfaces may carry default and static methods, but the no-state rule stands.
questions.pitfall: 'An interface is an abstract class without bodies.' The deeper differences — no state, multiple implementation, capability semantics — are the actual answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Abstract class vs interface — when would you choose each?
key_points: Abstract class for an is-a family sharing code and state: account types sharing balance logic.
Interface for a can-do capability cutting across unrelated families: Printable implemented by Invoice and Photo alike, or when a class needs several capabilities at once.
The one-liner: abstract class shares what things are; interface declares what things can do.
questions.pitfall: Listing differences without the when. The choice rule — shared code and state against cross-cutting capability — is what the question is actually asking.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the diamond problem?
key_points: With multiple class inheritance, if B and C both inherit from A and D inherits from both, D receives two paths to A's members — which version wins is ambiguous.
Java avoids it by forbidding multiple class inheritance; with Java 8 default methods a mild diamond returns, and the language forces D to override the conflicting method and choose explicitly.
questions.pitfall: Only 'Java does not allow multiple inheritance.' The reason is the diamond ambiguity, and the default-method footnote shows current knowledge.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Composition vs inheritance — why is composition often preferred?
key_points: Inheritance is is-a and couples the child to the parent's implementation — a parent change can silently break children, and the relationship is fixed at compile time.
Composition is has-a: build behaviour by holding components — a Car has an Engine — which couples only to interfaces, can be swapped at runtime and is far easier to test.
Inherit for genuine is-a; compose for everything else.
questions.pitfall: 'Inheritance is the OOP way so prefer it.' The coupling argument is the expected reasoning — favour composition unless the relationship is truly is-a.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Association vs aggregation vs composition.
key_points: Three strengths of has-a. Association: objects merely know each other — a Teacher and a Student.
Aggregation: whole-part where parts survive the whole — a Department has Professors who outlive it.
Composition: whole-part where parts die with the whole — a House and its Rooms.
Ownership and lifetime tighten at each step.
questions.pitfall: Treating aggregation and composition as synonyms. The lifetime test separates them — do the parts survive the whole? Professors yes, Rooms no.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are coupling and cohesion, and what should each be?
key_points: Coupling measures how much modules depend on each other's internals; cohesion measures how strongly one module's contents belong together.
Good design is low coupling and high cohesion: each class does one job fully and touches others only through narrow interfaces.
Most OOP advice — encapsulation, interfaces, composition — is in service of exactly this pair.
questions.pitfall: Reversing the goals. Low coupling, high cohesion — and tying the pair back to encapsulation shows the principles connect.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Upcasting, downcasting and instanceof.
key_points: Upcasting treats a child as its parent — Shape s = new Circle() — always safe and implicit; it is what enables polymorphic code.
Downcasting goes the other way to reach child-specific members — (Circle) s — and is checked at runtime: a wrong cast throws ClassCastException, so it is guarded with instanceof.
Frequent downcasting is also a design smell worth admitting.
questions.pitfall: Presenting downcasting as routine. It is the guarded exception, not the pattern — the instanceof guard and the design-smell remark complete the answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: State the constructor rules.
key_points: Same name as the class, no return type — not even void.
It runs at object creation to initialise state, can be overloaded, can call a sibling with this() or the parent with super() as the first statement, and can be private.
If you define no constructor the compiler supplies a default no-argument one; define any constructor and that default disappears.
questions.pitfall: 'A constructor returns the object.' It has no return type by definition — and forgetting that the default vanishes once you write any constructor is the classic compile-time surprise.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What happens to the default constructor when you define your own?
key_points: It is no longer generated. A class with only a parameterised constructor cannot be instantiated with new ClassName() unless you add the no-argument constructor back yourself — a frequent source of sudden compile errors when a constructor is added to an old class.
questions.pitfall: Assuming the default always exists. It exists only when no constructor is written — this exact scenario is a favourite quick check.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is constructor overloading and constructor chaining?
key_points: Overloading: several constructors with different parameter lists offering multiple ways to build the object.
Chaining: one constructor calling another — this(...) for a sibling in the same class, super(...) for the parent — as the first statement, so initialisation logic is written once and reused.
The parent's constructor always runs before the child's body.
questions.pitfall: Missing the first-statement rule. this() or super() must be the first line, and the parent-runs-first order is the follow-up detail.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a copy constructor?
key_points: A constructor taking an object of the same class and duplicating its state into the new one.
C++ provides it implicitly; in Java you write it by hand — public Account(Account other) — or use a clone or factory method.
The interview edge: mention shallow against deep copying of any referenced objects inside.
questions.pitfall: 'Java has copy constructors built in.' It does not — hand-written, and the shallow-versus-deep remark is where the extra mark sits.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Can a constructor be private, and why would it be?
key_points: Yes. A private constructor stops outside code from instantiating the class — the basis of the singleton pattern, where a static method returns the single shared instance, and of utility classes that are never meant to be instantiated at all.
Factory methods also use it to control creation.
questions.pitfall: 'Private constructor makes the class useless.' It makes creation controlled — singleton is the expected example, said with the static accessor.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: this vs super.
key_points: this refers to the current object — disambiguating fields from parameters, passing the object along, or this() calling a sibling constructor. super refers to the parent — super.method() reaching an overridden version, super.field, or super() calling the parent constructor, which must be the first statement.
Same-class against parent-class is the axis.
questions.pitfall: Using them interchangeably in constructor calls. this() chains within the class, super() chains to the parent — and only one of them, as the first line.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: static variables and methods — what does static mean?
key_points: Static members belong to the class, not to any object: one shared copy of a static variable across all instances, and static methods callable without an object.
Consequences: a static method has no this and cannot touch instance members directly.
Use for shared counters, constants and utility functions like Math.max.
questions.pitfall: 'Static means the value cannot change.' That is final. Static means class-owned — one copy, no this — and confusing the two keywords is a recorded miss.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Can we overload main()? Which one runs?
key_points: Yes — main is an ordinary method name and can be overloaded freely.
The JVM, however, invokes only the standard signature: public static void main(String[] args).
Other overloads run only if your code calls them explicitly.
questions.pitfall: 'No, main is special.' It overloads like any method; only the JVM's entry choice is fixed — the two-part answer is the complete one.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain the final keyword at its three levels.
key_points: A final variable is a constant — assigned once; for object references the reference is fixed though the object's state may still change.
A final method cannot be overridden — locking behaviour for subclasses.
A final class cannot be extended at all — String is the standard example, final for security and immutability.
questions.pitfall: Claiming a final reference freezes the object. It freezes the reference; the object may mutate — that nuance is precisely what the follow-up tests.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: static vs instance members — the practical difference.
key_points: Instance members live per object — each Account has its own balance.
Static members live once per class — a static accountCount is shared by all.
Access follows suit: instance members need an object; static members are reached through the class name.
Mixing them up — reading an instance field from a static method — is the compile error every beginner meets.
questions.pitfall: Explaining static by 'it loads first.' Ownership is the concept — class-owned against object-owned — and the shared-counter example lands it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Reproduce the access-modifier grid.
key_points: private: same class only. default (no modifier): same class and same package. protected: same class, same package and subclasses anywhere. public: everywhere.
Two tested edges: default stops at the package boundary even for subclasses, and protected reaches a subclass in another package — the two cells students misplace.
questions.pitfall: Guessing the protected and default cells. Those two are the entire reason the grid is asked — state them explicitly and the question is closed.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How do access modifiers enforce encapsulation?
key_points: By making the data unreachable except through the guarded path: fields go private, and the only access is through public methods that validate every change.
The compiler then guarantees no caller can bypass the rules — encapsulation stops being a convention and becomes enforced.
That link is the follow-up to the encapsulation pillar.
questions.pitfall: Treating getters and setters as ritual. A setter that validates is the guard; a blind setter is private theatre — say validation and the answer has substance.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why is String immutable in Java, and what follows from it?
key_points: Strings cannot change after creation.

Benefits: safe sharing across threads, safe use as map keys because hash codes never change, the string pool where identical literals share one object, and security — a filename cannot be mutated after validation.
Consequence: every 'modification' creates a new object, which is why loops that build strings need StringBuilder.
questions.pitfall: 'Immutable because Java says so.' The reasons — pooling, hashing, thread safety, security — are the answer, with StringBuilder as the practical corollary.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer.
key_points: String is immutable — each concatenation allocates a new object, so building in a loop is quadratic.
StringBuilder is the mutable builder — append in place, linear, the default choice.
StringBuffer is the synchronised twin — thread-safe and slower, relevant only when multiple threads share one builder, which is rare.
questions.pitfall: 'Always use StringBuffer to be safe.' Uncontended synchronisation is pure cost — StringBuilder is the default and the loop-concatenation trap is the motive.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: == vs equals() for objects.
key_points: == compares references — are these the same object in memory. equals() compares content — as defined by the class; String overrides it to compare characters.
Two equal-content strings from different sources can be == false and equals true; the string pool makes some literals == true, which is exactly why relying on == for strings is a bug.
questions.pitfall: Testing string equality with ==. It occasionally works because of the pool and fails in production — equals for content is the rule, said with the pool explanation.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why must equals() and hashCode() be overridden together?
key_points: Because hash-based collections depend on their contract: objects that are equal must return the same hash code, since a HashMap finds a key by hash bucket first and equals second.
Override equals alone and two 'equal' objects land in different buckets — the map stores duplicates and lookups miss.
Same fields in both methods, always together, is the rule.
questions.pitfall: Overriding equals and stopping. The broken-HashMap consequence is the reason this pair is asked — equal objects, different buckets, lost lookups.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are wrapper classes and autoboxing?
key_points: Wrappers are the object forms of primitives — Integer for int, Double for double — needed because collections and generics hold objects only.
Autoboxing converts automatically in both directions: an int dropped into a List<Integer> boxes itself.
Cautions: boxing in hot loops costs allocations, and == between wrappers compares references, not values, outside the small-value cache.
questions.pitfall: Ignoring the == trap. Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000; a == b is false — the wrapper comparison trap is the reason this question exists.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How does garbage collection work, and can you force it?
key_points: The JVM automatically reclaims objects no longer reachable from any live reference — freeing developers from manual deallocation and dangling-pointer bugs.
You can request collection with System.gc() but never command it; the JVM decides.
What you control is reachability: dropping references makes objects eligible.
questions.pitfall: 'System.gc() frees memory now.' It is a suggestion the JVM may ignore — eligibility through unreachability is the concept that scores.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Walk through try-catch-finally.
key_points: Risky code goes in try. A thrown exception jumps to the first matching catch, where it is handled. finally runs regardless of outcome — normal completion, caught exception or uncaught one — which makes it the home for cleanup such as closing resources.
Order matters in multi-catch: subclasses before superclasses, or the broad catch swallows everything.
questions.pitfall: Placing catch(Exception) first. It shadows every specific handler — specific before general is the ordering rule the panel checks.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Does finally always run? Name the edge cases.
key_points: Effectively yes — after normal completion, after a caught exception and even after a return statement in try, with finally executing before the method actually returns.
The only real exceptions: the JVM dying — System.exit or a crash — or an infinite loop before it.
The return-then-finally ordering is the tested edge.
questions.pitfall: 'finally is skipped when try returns.' It is not — finally runs before the return completes, and that exact behaviour is the favourite trick question.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions.
key_points: Checked exceptions extend Exception and the compiler forces handling or declaration — IOException, SQLException — representing recoverable external failures.
Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and need no declaration — NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBounds — representing programming bugs better fixed than caught.
Compiler-enforced against not is the mechanical difference; external failure against bug is the design difference.
questions.pitfall: Sorting by severity. The split is compile-time enforcement, not seriousness — an unchecked NPE can be as fatal as any checked failure.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: throw vs throws.
key_points: throw is a statement that raises one exception object right here: throw new IllegalArgumentException(...). throws is a declaration in the method signature listing the checked exceptions the method may pass to its caller.
One acts, the other warns — and only checked exceptions need the warning.
questions.pitfall: Using the words interchangeably. Statement against signature declaration — a one-line distinction that is asked verbatim and lost surprisingly often.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What happens if an exception is never caught?
key_points: It propagates up the call stack, method by method, running each finally on the way.
If it reaches the top of the thread uncaught, the thread terminates and the JVM prints the stack trace — the familiar crash.
That propagation is also the design: handle where you can act meaningfully, let it rise where you cannot.
questions.pitfall: 'The program hangs.' It terminates the thread with a stack trace — and the handle-where-meaningful principle turns the mechanics into design sense.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why create custom exceptions?
key_points: To speak the domain's language: InsufficientBalanceException tells the caller exactly what failed and can carry relevant fields, where a bare RuntimeException says nothing.
Extend Exception for recoverable, declared conditions or RuntimeException for programming violations, and keep the hierarchy shallow.
Meaningful failure types are API design, not decoration.
questions.pitfall: 'Built-in exceptions are enough.' A domain failure deserves a domain name — the InsufficientBalance example makes the case in one line.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Can static, private or final methods be overridden?
key_points: None of them, each for its own reason.
Static methods belong to the class — a same-signature static in the child is method hiding, resolved by reference type, not overriding.
Private methods are invisible to the child — a same-name method is simply new.
Final methods are explicitly locked by the parent.
Three no's, three different reasons — give all three.
questions.pitfall: One blanket 'no.' The reasons differ — hiding, invisibility, prohibition — and the static-hiding case with its reference-type resolution is the depth marker.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is method hiding?
key_points: When a child declares a static method with the same signature as the parent's static method.
It does not override — which version runs is decided by the reference type at compile time, not the object.
Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod() runs the parent's version — the opposite of overriding's behaviour, which is the entire point of the question.
questions.pitfall: Calling it overriding for statics. The resolution flips — reference type decides, not object — and that flip is what the panel is testing.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the singleton pattern and how is it built?
key_points: A class guaranteed to have exactly one instance with a global access point.
Construction: a private constructor blocks outside creation, a private static field holds the instance and a public static getInstance() returns it.
Mention the thread-safety wrinkle — lazy initialisation needs synchronisation or an eagerly created instance — and the answer reads senior.
questions.pitfall: Reciting getInstance without the private constructor. The private constructor is the enforcing mechanism — without it the pattern is a suggestion.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Shallow copy vs deep copy.
key_points: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares every referenced object inside — change the inner list through the copy and the original sees it.
A deep copy duplicates the whole graph, inner objects included, giving full independence at the cost of more work.
Java's default clone is shallow; deep copying is deliberate.
questions.pitfall: Assuming a copy is independent. Shared inner references are the trap — the change-through-the-copy example makes the difference visible.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is SOLID, in one line per letter?
key_points: Single responsibility — one reason to change per class.
Open-closed — open to extension, closed to modification.
Liskov substitution — a child must work anywhere its parent does.
Interface segregation — many small interfaces over one fat one.
Dependency inversion — depend on abstractions, not concretions.
One line each is the expected depth; going deeper is invited only if the panel pulls.
questions.pitfall: Expanding the acronym without meanings. The five one-liners are the deliverable — and Liskov is the one most often garbled, so rehearse it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What did Java 8 change for interfaces?
key_points: Interfaces may now carry default methods — implementations subclasses inherit and may override — and static methods.
The motive was evolving published interfaces without breaking every implementer.
The no-state rule still stands, and a class inheriting the same default from two interfaces must override and choose — the mild return of the diamond.
questions.pitfall: 'Interfaces can do everything abstract classes can now.' Still no instance state — that boundary keeps the abstract-class question alive.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
key_points: Strictly pass-by-value — always.
For objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference: the method can mutate the object both variables point to, but reassigning the parameter inside the method changes nothing outside.
That distinction — mutate yes, reassign no — resolves every confusing example thrown at this question.
questions.pitfall: 'Objects are passed by reference.' The reference is passed by value — the mutate-versus-reassign test is the proof, and stating it ends the debate.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: How do you answer 'explain OOP with an example from your project'?
key_points: Pick one class and walk the pillars through it in four sentences.
In our fee-management project, Payment kept its amount private with validated methods — encapsulation.
Callers used processPayment without knowing the gateway — abstraction.
CardPayment and UpiPayment extended Payment — inheritance.
The reconciler called process on a Payment list and each ran its own version — polymorphism.
Prepared per project, this is a closing statement; improvised, it is a stumble.
questions.pitfall: Reciting textbook Car-and-Engine examples. The question exists to hear your project — one class, four pillars, four sentences, prepared in advance.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, OOP Concepts (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the SDLC? Walk the phases with an output each.
key_points: The software development life cycle — the structured path from idea to retired system.

Requirements produce the SRS; design produces the architecture and detailed design; implementation produces code; testing produces a verified build with defect reports; deployment puts it in production; maintenance keeps it healthy and evolving.
The phase-plus-output pairing is what turns a list into an answer.
questions.pitfall: Naming phases without outputs. Each phase exists to produce something — SRS, design, code, verified build — and the outputs are the substance.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is an SRS and what makes a good requirement?
key_points: The Software Requirements Specification — the agreed record of what the system must do and how well, the contract design and testing are built against.
A good requirement is clear, testable and unambiguous: 'login responds within two seconds under a thousand concurrent users' can be verified; 'the system should be fast' cannot.
questions.pitfall: 'A document listing features.' Testability is the quality bar — give the fast-versus-two-seconds contrast and the point makes itself.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Functional vs non-functional requirements.
key_points: Functional requirements say what the system does — login, search, generate the receipt.
Non-functional requirements say how well it does it — performance, security, availability, usability.
From a fee-payment project: processing a payment is functional; completing it within three seconds and encrypting card data are non-functional.
One of each from your own project is the expected finish.
questions.pitfall: Examples only for the functional side. The NFR example is the half students miss — have performance or security from your project ready.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain the Waterfall model and where it fits.
key_points: Strictly sequential phases, each completed and signed off before the next begins — requirements frozen first, testing at the end.
Strengths: predictability, clear milestones, documentation.
Weakness: change is expensive and defects surface late.
It fits when requirements are genuinely stable and understood — regulated, contractual or safety-critical work.
questions.pitfall: 'Waterfall is obsolete.' It fits stable-requirement domains — the fits-when clause is what separates evaluation from fashion.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the V-model?
key_points: Waterfall bent into a V: every development phase on the left pairs with a test phase on the right — requirements pair with acceptance testing, design with system testing, detailed design with integration, coding with unit tests.
The message is that test planning starts with its paired phase, not after coding — verification and validation meet at the point of the V.
questions.pitfall: Describing it as 'Waterfall with more testing.' The pairing is the idea — each left phase writes the tests for its right partner, early.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the Spiral model?
key_points: Risk-driven iterations, each looping through plan, risk analysis, build and evaluate — often with a prototype retiring the biggest current risk.
Each loop grows the product while shrinking uncertainty.
It suits large, expensive projects where the dominant question is what might sink this, at the cost of heavy process and risk-analysis skill.
questions.pitfall: Reducing it to 'iterative development.' Risk analysis each loop is the differentiator — Spiral without the word risk is not Spiral.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Iterative vs incremental development.
key_points: Iterative refines the whole product in repeated passes — a rough complete sketch improved each cycle.
Incremental delivers the product in usable slices — module by module, each finished.
The painting analogy: iterative sketches the full canvas and refines everywhere; incremental completes one corner at a time.
Agile deliberately combines both — small increments, iteratively improved.
questions.pitfall: Using the words as synonyms. Refine-the-whole against add-finished-pieces is the split, and the painting picture makes it stick.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the Prototype model and when is it right?
key_points: Build a quick throwaway version first so users can react to something concrete, then write real requirements from what was learned.
Right when requirements are foggy — users who cannot specify a screen can always criticise one.
The discipline: the prototype is for learning and is thrown away; shipping it is how prototype code becomes production debt.
questions.pitfall: Skipping the throwaway discipline. 'The prototype must be discarded' is the professional half of this answer — shipped prototypes are the classic origin of legacy pain.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is Agile, and what do its values actually mean?
key_points: Iterative delivery in short increments with continuous feedback, welcoming change over following a frozen plan.

The values weigh working software over exhaustive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation and responding to change over the plan — weigh, not replace: documentation and plans still exist, sized to what earns its keep.
questions.pitfall: 'Agile means no documentation and no planning.' The values are preferences, not prohibitions — saying 'over, not instead of' corrects the most common Agile error aloud.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Agile vs Waterfall — when is each right?
key_points: Waterfall when requirements are stable and change is costly — regulated or contractual builds where the spec is the contract.
Agile when requirements will evolve and early feedback matters — products discovering what users want.
The deciding question is the rate of requirement change; neither is universally right, and one example each way completes the answer.
questions.pitfall: Crowning Agile universally. The panel wants the decision rule — requirement stability — not a fashion verdict.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain Scrum in one breath, then its roles.
key_points: Scrum organises Agile work into fixed sprints of two to four weeks with a small set of ceremonies and three roles.
Product Owner owns the what — the backlog and its priorities.
Scrum Master owns the how — the process, removing blockers, protecting the team.
The Development Team owns the build and self-organises around the sprint goal.
questions.pitfall: Making the Scrum Master a manager. The role serves and unblocks — servant leadership, not command — and that correction is a favourite follow-up.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Walk the Scrum ceremonies.
key_points: Sprint planning selects what fits from the backlog and shapes the sprint goal.
The daily stand-up is fifteen minutes of done, next and blocked.
The sprint review demonstrates the increment to stakeholders for feedback.
The retrospective turns the team inward — what worked, what did not, what changes next sprint.
Review inspects the product; retrospective inspects the process.
questions.pitfall: Merging review and retrospective. Product-facing against process-facing is the separation, and it is asked exactly that way.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Product backlog vs sprint backlog.
key_points: The product backlog is everything wanted, ordered by the Product Owner's priorities — a living list, never finished.
The sprint backlog is the slice the team committed to for this sprint, plus the plan to deliver it — owned by the team and stable within the sprint.
Whole wish-list against this fortnight's commitment.
