questions.pitfall: 'Two names for the task list.' Different owners, different lifetimes, different scope — the three axes are the answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a user story, and what are acceptance criteria?
key_points: A user story is a requirement in user language: as a role, I want a capability, so that a benefit — as a student, I want to download my hall ticket so that I can enter the exam.
Acceptance criteria are the testable conditions that define done for that story — logged-in students only, PDF format, available till exam day.
Stories carry the intent; criteria carry the test.
questions.pitfall: A story without the so-that or without criteria. The benefit clause carries the why, and the criteria are what testing runs against — both halves count.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Story points and velocity.
key_points: Story points size relative effort and complexity — this story is roughly twice that one — deliberately not hours, so estimates survive individual speed differences.
Velocity is the points a team actually completes per sprint; after a few sprints it stabilises and becomes the planning yardstick for what fits next.
Points size the work; velocity measures the team.
questions.pitfall: Converting points to hours in the answer. The relative-not-absolute nature is the concept — and 'my project's velocity settled near eight' is the evidence sentence.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is the Definition of Done?
key_points: The team's agreed checklist a story must pass before it counts — typically coded, reviewed, tested, integrated and deployed to the demo environment.
It exists to kill the ninety-percent-done illusion: a story is done or it is not, by the same public standard every time.
questions.pitfall: 'Done means the developer finished coding.' The whole point is that coding alone is not done — the shared checklist is the definition.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Scrum vs Kanban.
key_points: Scrum batches work into fixed sprints with committed scope and ceremonies — rhythm and predictability.
Kanban flows work continuously across a visual board with work-in-progress limits — no sprints, optimise flow and cycle time.
Scrum fits feature development; Kanban fits support and operations where work arrives continuously.
WIP limits are Kanban's engine — starting new work is forbidden until current work moves.
questions.pitfall: Kanban described as 'Scrum without meetings.' The WIP limit is Kanban's defining mechanism — without it a board is just a to-do list.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Narrate one sprint of your own project in Scrum vocabulary.
key_points: The shape panels accept: our product backlog held about forty stories; in planning we committed twelve points to the sprint goal of online fee receipts; daily stand-ups surfaced a payment-gateway blocker our Scrum Master chased; the review demoed receipts to our guide; the retrospective moved us to smaller stories; velocity settled near eight.
One rehearsed paragraph — this converts the entire subject into evidence.
questions.pitfall: Generic textbook narration. The panel is listening for your numbers and your blocker — prepare the paragraph per project; it cannot be improvised.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Why is testing a separate discipline — what is it for?
key_points: To find defects before users do and to give evidence the system meets its requirements.
Testing cannot prove the absence of bugs — it reduces risk by hunting them systematically where they are most likely and most damaging.
That framing — risk reduction with evidence, not proof of perfection — is the professional answer.
questions.pitfall: 'Testing makes the software bug-free.' No amount of testing proves absence — risk reduction is the honest and expected claim.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Verification vs validation.
key_points: Verification asks: are we building the product right — reviews, walkthroughs and static checks against the design, largely before and during construction.
Validation asks: are we building the right product — executing tests against actual user needs.
Verification catches deviation from spec; validation catches a spec that missed the need. Verification comes first.
questions.pitfall: Merging them into 'testing.' The two questions — right-way against right-thing — are the answer, with which-comes-first as the standard follow-up.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: QA vs QC.
key_points: Quality assurance is process-oriented and preventive — standards, reviews and audits that stop defects from being created.
Quality control is product-oriented and detective — testing the built product to find defects that got through.
QA improves how work is done; QC checks what was done.
Prevention against detection is the one-line version.
questions.pitfall: Treating QA as a fancier word for testing. Testing is QC; QA is the process discipline around it — the prevention-detection axis separates them.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Error vs defect vs failure.
key_points: An error is the human mistake — the wrong line written.
A defect, or bug, is that mistake sitting in the code.
A failure is the defect executing in front of a user — wrong output, crash, corruption.
The chain matters because a defect can exist without ever failing: dead code holds defects that never run.
questions.pitfall: Using the three words interchangeably. The chain — mistake, flaw, manifestation — plus the dead-code observation is the full answer.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Test case vs test scenario.
key_points: A scenario is the high-level what to test: verify login functionality.
A test case is the precise how: steps, specific inputs, preconditions and the expected result for one path — valid user with wrong password sees the error message and no session.
One scenario expands into many cases covering its paths.
questions.pitfall: Writing a case without an expected result. Without the expected result there is nothing to compare against — it is the field that makes a case a test.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Walk the defect lifecycle. Who closes a defect?
key_points: New when reported, Assigned to a developer, Open under investigation, Fixed when the change is made, Retest when it returns to the tester, then Closed if the fix holds or Reopened if not — with side exits: Rejected as not-a-defect, Duplicate or Deferred to a later release.
The tester closes the defect, after retesting — never the developer who fixed it.
questions.pitfall: Letting the developer close it. Independent confirmation is the point of the lifecycle — the tester closes, and that is the exact question.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Severity vs priority, with a mismatch example each way.
key_points: Severity is technical impact — how badly the defect breaks the system.
Priority is business urgency — how soon it must be fixed.
High severity, low priority: a crash in a legacy module nobody uses.
Low severity, high priority: the client's name misspelt on the homepage before tomorrow's launch.
The tester gauges severity; the business sets priority.
questions.pitfall: 'They are basically the same.' The two mismatch examples are the required proof — this pair is asked verbatim, season after season.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What goes into a test plan?
key_points: The strategy document for the testing effort: scope — what is and is not tested; approach and techniques; entry and exit criteria; environment and data needs; schedule and responsibilities; risks with contingencies; and the deliverables.
The two items panels probe are scope's exclusions and the exit criteria — how you know testing is done.
questions.pitfall: A vague 'document describing testing.' Naming entry and exit criteria and the out-of-scope list shows a plan has actually been seen.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are entry and exit criteria?
key_points: Entry criteria gate the start of a test phase — build deployed, smoke test passed, test data ready — so effort is not wasted on an untestable build.
Exit criteria define completion — planned cases executed, pass rate met, no open critical defects — so 'done' is a measured state, not a feeling.
Together they bound the phase objectively.
questions.pitfall: 'Testing ends when time runs out.' That happens, but the answer is the defined exit bar — measured completion is what the term exists for.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Walk the four testing levels.
key_points: Unit testing checks the smallest pieces in isolation, by developers.
Integration testing checks that combined modules talk correctly — interfaces are where systems break.
System testing exercises the complete integrated product against requirements, end to end.
Acceptance testing lets the customer confirm the product fits the need — alpha in-house, beta with real users.
Scope widens and the tester changes at each level.
questions.pitfall: Jumping straight to system testing as 'the real testing.' The ladder and who tests at each rung is the structure the question wants.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are the integration testing approaches?
key_points: Big bang joins everything at once and tests — simple, but failures are hard to localise.

Incremental integrates piece by piece: top-down starts from high-level modules using stubs for the missing lower ones; bottom-up starts from the base using drivers to simulate callers; the sandwich combines both.
Incremental wins because each new failure points at the newest joint.
questions.pitfall: Only defining integration testing. The approaches with stubs and drivers are the content — and stub-versus-driver is its own follow-up.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Regression vs retesting.
key_points: Retesting re-runs the exact failed case after a fix to confirm that defect is gone — targeted, cannot be skipped.
Regression re-runs a broader suite after any change to catch side-effects elsewhere — the safety net, and the first thing worth automating because it repeats forever.
Confirm-the-fix against catch-the-fallout.
questions.pitfall: 'Both mean testing again.' Different targets — the fixed defect against everything around it — and regression-is-automated-first is the standard follow-up.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Smoke vs sanity testing.
key_points: Smoke is broad and shallow on a new build — do the major functions basically work, is the build worth testing at all; it runs first and gates deeper testing.
Sanity is narrow and deep after a small change — does the changed area behave rationally.
Build-health check against focused recheck; smoke first, always.
questions.pitfall: Using the terms interchangeably. Breadth against depth plus which-runs-first — the exact two points this verbatim question scores on.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Functional vs non-functional testing.
key_points: Functional testing verifies what the system does against requirements — features, flows, calculations.
Non-functional testing verifies how well — performance, load, stress, security, usability, compatibility.
A payment that succeeds is functional evidence; a payment that succeeds in under three seconds with ten thousand concurrent users is non-functional evidence.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting non-functional examples. Naming performance, security and usability as the how-well family is what completes the split.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Load vs stress vs volume testing.
key_points: Load testing measures behaviour at expected demand — response times under the traffic the system was designed for.
Stress testing pushes beyond design limits to find the breaking point and to watch how it fails — graceful degradation or collapse.
Volume testing loads the data dimension — millions of rows — where indexes and queries buckle.
Expected demand, beyond limits, data size.
questions.pitfall: One blob called 'performance testing.' The three probe different failure modes — the three-phrase summary keeps them apart under follow-up.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Black-box vs white-box testing.
key_points: Black-box tests from the outside — inputs against expected outputs, no knowledge of code; its techniques are equivalence partitioning, boundary values and decision tables.
White-box tests with the code open — designing cases to cover statements, branches and paths.
They complement: black-box asks does it meet the spec; white-box asks did we exercise the code.
questions.pitfall: Ranking one above the other. They answer different questions and coexist at different levels — complementarity is the accepted verdict.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Alpha vs beta testing.
key_points: Both are acceptance-stage tests by real users.
Alpha runs in-house — users at the developer's site, environment controlled, defects handled immediately.
Beta runs in the wild — real users in real environments, feedback flowing back at scale before general release.
Controlled inside against uncontrolled outside is the whole distinction.
questions.pitfall: Placing alpha with developers-testing-their-own-code. Alpha is user acceptance conducted in-house — users test, developers observe — location and control are the variables.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is exploratory testing and when does it add value?
key_points: Simultaneous learning, test design and execution — an experienced tester probes the product without scripted cases, guided by risk and curiosity.
It finds the defects scripts never imagined, especially in usability and unusual flows, and it shines early when specs are thin.
It complements scripted testing rather than replacing it — coverage still needs the scripts.
questions.pitfall: Dismissing it as 'random clicking.' It is skilled, risk-guided investigation — the complement-not-replacement framing keeps the answer professional.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain equivalence partitioning with an example.
key_points: Divide inputs into classes the system should treat identically, then test one value per class instead of hundreds.
An age field accepting 18 to 60 has three partitions — below 18 invalid, 18 to 60 valid, above 60 invalid — so 10, 35 and 70 cover what a thousand random values would.
The economy with preserved coverage is the point.
questions.pitfall: Testing many values from the same partition. One representative per class is the technique — more from the same class adds cost, not coverage.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Explain boundary value analysis for age 18 to 60.
key_points: Defects cluster at edges — off-by-one comparisons live exactly there — so test each boundary and its neighbours: 17, 18, 19 at the lower edge and 59, 60, 61 at the upper.
Six values that catch the >= written as > class of bugs.
BVA rides on top of equivalence partitioning: partition first, then attack each partition's edges.
questions.pitfall: Testing only 18 and 60. The neighbours — 17, 19, 59, 61 — are where off-by-one bugs surface, and the six-value answer is the expected form.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: When do decision tables beat other techniques?
key_points: When output depends on combinations of conditions — discount rules across member type, cart value and coupon.
The table enumerates every condition combination with its expected action, exposing the combinations the spec forgot.
Its power is systematic completeness over business-rule logic where partitioning single inputs misses the interactions.
questions.pitfall: Using it for a single-input field. Its territory is interacting conditions — the combinations-the-spec-forgot line is why it earns a place.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Statement coverage vs branch coverage.
key_points: Statement coverage: every line executed at least once.
Branch coverage: every decision taken both ways — the true and the false path of every if.
Branch is strictly stronger: one test can touch all lines of an if-without-else yet never exercise the false path where the bug hides.
Full branch implies full statement; never the reverse.
questions.pitfall: Treating 100% statement coverage as thorough. The untested false path is the classic counter-example — branch subsumes statement, and saying why scores.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is cyclomatic complexity?
key_points: A count of a function's independent paths, computed from the control-flow graph as E − N + 2P — or, practically, decisions plus one.
It sets the minimum tests needed for path-level confidence and doubles as a maintainability signal: a function scoring high is asking to be split.
A number that guides both testing and refactoring.
questions.pitfall: The formula with no use attached. Minimum test paths plus the refactor signal — the two applications are what make the metric worth knowing.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is ad-hoc testing and how does it differ from exploratory?
key_points: Ad-hoc is informal, undocumented testing without plan or structure — quick and occasionally lucky, but unrepeatable and unmeasurable.
Exploratory is also unscripted but disciplined: charters, time-boxes, notes and risk guidance.
The difference is intent and record — exploratory can be reviewed and repeated; ad-hoc leaves nothing behind.
questions.pitfall: Presenting them as the same freestyle. Discipline and documentation are the separators — charter and notes turn wandering into a technique.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What problem does version control solve?
key_points: It records every change with author, time and message, so the project has an inspectable history: any version can be recovered, changes can be compared and undone, and many developers can work in parallel without overwriting each other.
Without it, teams are emailing zip files and praying — history, recovery and parallel work are the three wins.
questions.pitfall: 'It backs up code.' Backup is incidental — history, comparison and safe parallel work are what the tool exists for.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Walk the basic Git flow.
key_points: Clone the repository, create a branch for the work, edit, stage with add, commit with a meaningful message — each commit a snapshot — push the branch to the remote, open a pull request for review and merge into the main branch.
Pull regularly to stay current.
Branch, commit, push, review, merge — one breath.
questions.pitfall: A commit message of 'changes.' The flow is expected fluently, and the meaningful-message habit is the professionalism marker inside it.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is branching and why is it central?
key_points: A branch is an independent line of development — features and fixes proceed in isolation while the main branch stays releasable.
Work merges back only when ready and reviewed.
Branching is what turns version control from a history tool into a collaboration model: parallel work without stepping on each other.
questions.pitfall: 'Branches are copies of the folder.' They are lightweight pointers into the same history — cheap to create, which is why one-branch-per-task works.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a merge conflict and how is it resolved?
key_points: When two branches changed the same lines, Git cannot choose and stops, marking the conflicting region in the file.
A human resolves it: open the file, decide what the combined truth is, remove the markers, stage and commit.
The professional habits that minimise conflicts: small branches, frequent pulls and early merges.
questions.pitfall: 'Git fixes conflicts automatically.' Git merges what it can; the same-lines case is precisely where a human must decide — that is the definition.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Merge vs rebase.
key_points: Merge joins two branches with a merge commit, preserving both histories exactly as they happened — safe and honest, at the cost of a busier graph.
Rebase replays your commits on top of the new base, producing a linear history — cleaner to read, but it rewrites commits, so the rule is never rebase branches others already share.
questions.pitfall: Recommending rebase everywhere for cleanliness. The rewriting risk on shared branches is the caveat that shows real usage — clean history has a rule attached.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What is a pull request?
key_points: The review gate: you propose your branch for merging, teammates read the diff, comment, request changes and approve; automated checks run alongside.
Only then does the code join the main branch.
The PR is where code review lives — quality control, knowledge sharing and a permanent record of why the change was made.
questions.pitfall: 'A request to pull code from the server.' That is git pull. The PR is a review-and-merge proposal — the collaboration gate, not the download command.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: Git vs GitHub.
key_points: Git is the version-control tool itself — distributed, running on your machine, fully functional offline.
GitHub is a hosting and collaboration service built around Git repositories — pull requests, issues, permissions, CI hooks.
Git would exist without GitHub; GitHub exists because Git did.
Tool against platform in one line.
questions.pitfall: Using the names interchangeably. GitLab and Bitbucket host Git too — naming an alternative platform proves the separation is understood.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)

questions.question: What are CI/CD and TDD, in interview depth?
key_points: Continuous Integration: every push triggers automated build and tests, so integration problems surface within minutes, not at release.
Continuous Delivery extends the pipeline until every passing build is deployable at the press of a button; Continuous Deployment presses it automatically.
TDD writes the failing test first, then the code to pass it, then refactors — red, green, refactor.
One breath each is the expected depth here.
questions.pitfall: Deep-diving unprompted. These close the subject at awareness depth — a crisp definition each, and let the panel pull if they want more.
questions.source: CCC Placement Review Series 2026, SDLC, Agile and Testing (user-supplied study material; sentences taken from the book)
